title: Arjuna asks to see (1.20–1.27)
hook: the greatest archer asks for his chariot between the armies, to get a good look at the enemy, and Krishna parks it in front of his grandfather
tomorrow: "I see no good in killing my kin" (1.28–1.39)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the armies: a blind king asking, conch shells roaring, and your line was the field. What field did you stand on? Today, Arjuna asks for one thing, and gets it. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

The conches have finished roaring. Arrows are about to fly. And Arjuna, the archer, lifts his bow. Over his chariot flies his banner, and on it is Hanuman, the monkey who carried a mountain, the one you met on this path. Arjuna turns to his driver, Krishna, and asks for something that sounds perfectly sensible. He wants a look. Drive me out between the two armies, he says, so I can see who I'm fighting. It's what any good commander would do. Check the other side. Size them up. Krishna says nothing. He just drives.
screen: `HANUMAN ON THE BANNER.` → `DRIVE ME OUT BETWEEN THEM.` → `KRISHNA JUST DRIVES.`

segments.voice: In Sanskrit, Arjuna's request is: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me 'chyuta. Between both armies, set my chariot, Achyuta, unfailing one. He wants to see, he says, those who've come to fight for Duryodhana. He's thinking of enemies. Now watch where Krishna stops. Sanjaya tells the king: Krishna drove the chariot between the armies, and set it down right in front of Bhishma and Drona. Bhishma, the great-uncle Arjuna grew up calling grandfather. Drona, the teacher who taught him to shoot. Of all the places on that huge field, Krishna parks there. And he says just one line, his first words in the whole Gita: Partha, look at these Kurus, gathered together. Look at them. Arjuna looks. And the text slows down and lists what he sees, one by one: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, friends, fathers-in-law. Every one of them is family, or nearly. He asked to see the enemy, and he saw his people. The verse says he was overcome with pity, and he began to speak, in sorrow. Notice what Krishna doesn't do. He doesn't argue, doesn't warn, doesn't explain. He doesn't say, are you sure? He just puts Arjuna exactly where he'll have to see the truth, and lets him look. A fight looks easy from a distance. The other side is a category: them. Drive out into the middle, stop in front of real faces, and the category falls apart. Everything the Gita says next starts from this moment. A man who asked to see, and saw too much.
screen: `SET MY CHARIOT BETWEEN THE ARMIES.` · `KRISHNA STOPS BEFORE BHISHMA, DRONA.` · `PARTHA, LOOK AT THEM.` · `HE ASKED FOR ENEMIES, SAW FAMILY.` · then, large: `LOOK AT THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drive out into the middle. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's on the other side of something with you. At work, at home, in the news. Right now they're probably a category in your mind: them. Now picture Krishna driving your chariot out and stopping right in front of them. Look at their face. Who raised them? Who are they a father, a sister, a grandchild to? What did they look like at ten? You don't have to agree with them. Just look, and let them be a person for a minute. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna asks to see. He asks for his chariot between the armies, and Krishna stops it in front of the people he loves.
Your line: look at them. Today, when someone becomes a them in your head, stop, and picture their face up close. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Readers of the Gita often pause on 1.21–1.27, where Krishna drives Arjuna's chariot between the armies and stops before Bhishma and Drona; some readers hear Krishna's first words, telling Arjuna to look, as the quiet start of all that follows.

fork.setup: you're Krishna, driving. Arjuna wants to see the enemy. the field is huge. where do you stop the chariot?
options: in front of Bhishma and Drona.
fork.reveal: right in front of the great-uncle he called grandfather and the teacher who trained him. then: look at them.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 1.21: between both armies. Arjuna's request.

trapdoor: what you thought: a general checking the other side.
what it means: Arjuna asks to see enemies, and Krishna parks him in front of his family. he sees his people.
what a scholar hears: Krishna's first words in the Gita are just 'look', and the verse then lists every relation Arjuna sees.

sources.quoted: senayor ubhayor madhye ratham sthapaya me 'chyuta

notes: Hanuman on Arjuna's banner (kapidhvaja), 1.20. Confirm the tie-back to the Hanuman week (days 29–35).
Krishna 'sets it down in front of Bhishma and Drona and all the kings' (1.25). Confirm.

Krishna's first words in the Gita, 1.25: 'Partha, behold these Kurus gathered together'; paraphrased as 'look at these Kurus, gathered together'. Confirm the claim they are his first words (he blows his conch in 1.14 but does not speak).
Achyuta glossed as 'unshakable one' (lit. 'the unfallen'). Confirm.

Editor review 2026-10-01: cut 'the finest archer alive'; Achyuta glossed 'unfailing one'; Bhishma no longer said to have 'raised' Arjuna (now the great-uncle he called grandfather); cut stock 'quietly brilliant' and 'most of our fights'; how-it's-done no longer claims commentaries treat 1.25 as the start of the teaching (day 161 gives that to 2.7).
